questions.question: Under 21 CFR 210.1(b), how does the law regard a drug if the methods used in, or the facilities or controls for, its manufacture, processing, packing, or holding do not comply with the CGMP regulations such as Parts 210 and 211?

options.A: As only an administrative lapse, regarded as a violation only if an actual quality defect is found by testing
options.B: As misbranded, which must be corrected before the next inspection before the drug can continue to be marketed
options.C: As adulterated, with regulatory action against both the drug and the persons responsible
options.D: As not meeting the registered specifications, with the quality unit alone deciding whether to release the batch, and the batch may continue to be sold as usual before the internal investigation is completed

questions.explanation: Section 210.1 provides that failure to comply with CGMP causes the drug to be regarded as adulterated, and regulatory action may be taken against the drug and the persons responsible. This is independent of whether the drug actually caused harm or passed testing, so the idea that it is "only an administrative lapse, a violation only if an actual quality defect is found by testing" is wrong.

questions.question: A company manufactures an investigational drug for a Phase 1 study. Under 21 CFR 210.2(c), how does Part 211 apply to this drug?

options.A: In principle Part 211 does not apply, but it does apply if the drug is supplied for Phase 2 or Phase 3 studies
options.B: All provisions of Part 211 always apply, with no exceptions or exemptions by study phase, even if the drug is used only in early Phase 1 safety studies
options.C: It begins to apply only after the drug is approved for marketing, and clinical trial phases before that are not regulated
options.D: Only the laboratory controls provisions apply, and the remaining provisions apply only after Phase 3 is complete

questions.explanation: Section 210.2 states that Part 211 does not apply to the manufacture of investigational drugs for Phase 1 studies, although the regulatory requirements for safety still apply; once the drug is supplied for Phase 2 or Phase 3 studies, Part 211 applies.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 210.3, what is the key point of the definition of lot number (lot number / control number / batch number)?

options.A: A code indicating the manufacturing date and expiration date, whose format is set by each plant and need not allow tracing of batch history
options.B: A serial number in a format specified by the regulatory authority, covering only the stage from receipt of raw materials to completion of manufacture of the finished product
options.C: An alphabetical code issued by the quality unit to indicate the release status and test results of the batch
options.D: Any distinctive combination of letters, numbers, or symbols from which the complete history of the manufacture to distribution of the batch can be determined

questions.explanation: The key point of the definition in 210.3 is traceability: the lot number allows the complete history of the manufacture, processing, packing, holding, and distribution of the batch to be determined. A date marking alone or coverage of only the manufacturing stage does not meet the definition.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 210.3, which particulate contaminant is defined as a fiber?

options.A: Any foreign matter visible to the naked eye that must be rejected during visual inspection, regardless of its length-to-width ratio
options.B: Any particulate contaminant with a length at least three times its width, regardless of material or source
options.C: Any particulate contaminant with a length at least twice its width that must come from material shed from a filter
options.D: All particles with a diameter smaller than the filter pore size, including crystals chemically precipitated from solution

questions.explanation: Section 210.3 defines a fiber geometrically: any particulate contaminant with a length at least three times its width. It is not limited by visibility or by origin from filter media, so the other descriptions (visible to the naked eye, a ratio of two with filter origin, defined by pore size) are not the regulatory definition.

questions.question: The theoretical yield of a process stage is 1,000 vials and the actual yield is 950 vials. Under 21 CFR 210.3, what is the percentage of theoretical yield for this stage?

options.A: About 105%, that is, the theoretical yield divided by the actual yield
options.B: 5%, the proportion of the difference between theoretical and actual yield
options.C: 95%, the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, expressed as a percentage
options.D: 50%, the average of the actual and theoretical yields divided by the theoretical yield

questions.explanation: Section 210.3 defines it as the ratio of the actual yield to the theoretical yield at the same stage, expressed as a percentage, so it is 950/1,000 = 95%. The "about 105%" figure inverts the numerator and denominator, and "5%" is the loss proportion.

questions.question: A company contracts another company to manufacture a finished product. Under 21 CFR 211.22, who is responsible for approving or rejecting these contract-manufactured drug products?

options.A: The production manager of the contract manufacturer, because the product was manufactured and packaged in the contract manufacturer's facility
options.B: The contracting company's own quality control unit (QCU), which is responsible for approving or rejecting drug products manufactured under contract
options.C: An external auditor jointly engaged by both parties, whose opinion is regarded as completing the approval
options.D: The regulatory authority, which will rule at the next inspection, with interim release agreed between the parties until then

questions.explanation: Section 211.22 states explicitly that the QCU is responsible for approving or rejecting drug products manufactured, processed, packed, or held under contract by another company; responsibility cannot be transferred by outsourcing.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT something the quality control unit is responsible for approving or rejecting under 21 CFR 211.22?

options.A: Drug product containers and closures, which must be approved or rejected by the QCU before use
options.B: Packaging materials and labeling, which must be approved or rejected by the QCU before use
options.C: In-process materials, which must be approved or rejected by the QCU before release
options.D: The purchasing budget for production equipment and supplier price negotiation terms, with the QCU deciding the amounts and vendors

questions.explanation: Section 211.22 lists what the QCU must approve or reject: components, containers, closures, in-process materials, packaging materials, labeling, and drug products, and it may also review production records. Purchasing budgets and price negotiation are not within the provision.

questions.question: A plant's SOP requires the QCU to review all batch records, but in practice this procedure is often not followed. Under 21 CFR 211.22, what kind of problem is this?

options.A: A violation of the requirement that written procedures be followed; a mismatch between procedure and actual practice is a deficiency
options.B: As long as the SOP has been approved and filed, it complies, and the timing of actual execution is at the plant's discretion
options.C: As long as the SOP text is changed to match current practice it is not a deficiency, and no explanation is needed
options.D: It is a matter of consultant qualifications and records, unrelated to QCU responsibilities or the requirement for written procedures

questions.explanation: Section 211.22 requires that the responsibilities and procedures of the QCU be in writing, and that the written procedures be followed. Having an SOP is not enough; a mismatch between actual practice and the documents is a deficiency.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.25, how should CGMP training be conducted?

options.A: Once at hire, and afterward employees only read announcements on their own when regulations are revised
options.B: Taught by the direct supervisor based on personal experience, with no specific qualifications and no need to cover written procedures
options.C: Conducted on a continuing basis by qualified individuals, with sufficient frequency to ensure employees remain familiar with the CGMP requirements applicable to them
options.D: Attended only by production line operators once a year at a fixed time, with a written test required before going on the line, and not conducted by qualified individuals or on a continuing basis

questions.explanation: Section 211.25 requires CGMP training to be conducted by qualified individuals on a continuing basis, with sufficient frequency to ensure that employees remain familiar with the requirements applicable to their functions; the provision does not set a fixed number of sessions and is not limited to particular staff.

questions.question: An operator has a clearly visible open lesion on the hand. Under 21 CFR 211.28, which of the following actions is correct?

options.A: After putting on double gloves, the operator may continue weighing raw materials and handling in-process materials
options.B: Reassign the operator to weigh raw materials, because only people who contact the finished product must be excluded from direct contact
options.C: Move the operator to the packaging line, because packaging is not within the scope of direct contact that must be excluded
options.D: The operator must not have direct contact with product or materials until the condition is corrected or a competent medical person determines that quality is not affected

questions.explanation: Section 211.28 requires that a person with an apparent illness or open lesions be excluded from direct contact with components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, and drug products until the condition is corrected or determined by competent medical personnel not to jeopardize the safety or quality of the product.

questions.question: 21 CFR 211.42 requires that buildings have sufficient space for the orderly placement of equipment and materials. What is the main purpose of this requirement?

options.A: To prevent mix-ups between different components, containers, closures, labeling, in-process materials, or drug products, and to prevent contamination
options.B: To minimize the distance personnel travel, to raise output per shift and reduce labor cost and equipment idle time, regardless of whether materials or labels might be mixed up
options.C: To ensure that every production line can make a different drug at the same time, without needing to consider segregation of materials and labeling
options.D: To avoid needing approval when expanding equipment later, and to keep the plant tidy for outside visits

questions.explanation: The space requirement in 211.42 is intended to prevent mix-ups and contamination, and the flow of materials and drug products must also be designed to prevent contamination; capacity or expansion is not the purpose of the provision.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.42, which of the following must the air supply to aseptic processing areas meet?

options.A: Filtered through primary filters only, and maintained at negative pressure relative to the outside to prevent contaminated air from escaping
options.B: HEPA-filtered and necessarily unidirectional (laminar) flow; non-unidirectional flow is not accepted by the regulation, and if non-unidirectional it may be used only after separate approval
options.C: HEPA-filtered and maintained under positive pressure, whether the flow is laminar or nonlaminar
options.D: HEPA-filtered, with positive or negative pressure left to be decided according to product toxicity and the plant's experience

questions.explanation: Section 211.42 requires that air be HEPA-filtered under positive pressure, and states explicitly that the flow may be either laminar or nonlaminar; the claim that only unidirectional flow is allowed is therefore wrong.

questions.question: What does 21 CFR 211.46 require of the air handling systems used for the manufacture, processing, and packing of penicillin?

options.A: They may be shared with other human drug products, with only an extra primary filter added where penicillin enters
options.B: They must be completely separate from those used for other human drug products and not shared
options.C: They need to be isolated from the systems for other drugs only while penicillin processing is under way, and may be shared the rest of the time
options.D: They may be shared with other drugs, provided cleaning validation is completed and records are kept each time the product changes

questions.explanation: Section 211.46 requires that the air handling systems for penicillin be completely separate from those for other human drug products, and not partly isolated or replaced by cleaning controls.

questions.question: An injectable manufacturing process truly cannot avoid using a filter that releases fibers. Under 21 CFR 211.72, what additional measure is required afterward?

options.A: Add an asbestos filter medium to adsorb the shed fibers, and note the source lot of the filter medium in the batch record
options.B: Connect a second fiber-releasing filter of the same type but larger pore size in series for double filtration to reduce fibers, and note the model and usage count of the filter in the batch record
options.C: Simply record the fiber content of each batch and explain it at release, with no additional filtration step
options.D: A non-fiber-releasing filter with a maximum mean pore size of 0.22 micron (0.45 micron if manufacturing conditions require) must be used afterward

questions.explanation: Section 211.72 in principle prohibits the use of fiber-releasing filters for injectable products unless manufacture is not possible without them; if they must be used, an additional non-fiber-releasing filter of 0.22 micron (or 0.45 micron where conditions require) must follow. Asbestos filter media are expressly prohibited.

questions.question: Before changing production batches, which of the following should the written equipment cleaning procedure include under 21 CFR 211.67, to avoid confusion of batch information and confirm cleanliness status?

options.A: Removal or obliteration of the previous batch identification, and inspection of the equipment for cleanliness immediately before use
options.B: Retention of the previous batch identification for later traceability, and a cleanliness inspection within one week before use is enough
options.C: Cleaning just before use is enough, with no need to assign responsible persons or set schedules for cleaning and maintenance
options.D: Cleaned equipment needs no special protection and can be left in the production area until the next batch, without inspection

questions.explanation: Section 211.67 requires cleaning procedures that include assignment of responsibility, schedules, removal or obliteration of previous batch identification, protection of cleaned equipment, and inspection of equipment for cleanliness immediately before use. The other descriptions are contrary to the provision.

questions.question: A newly received lot of raw material has not yet been tested or examined. Under 21 CFR 211.82, how should this lot be handled?

options.A: It may first be used in a low-risk batch, and release formalities and records are completed after the test results are available
options.B: After the warehouse operator judges that it looks normal, it may be moved to the released materials area for production to draw
options.C: It is regarded as released once sampling is complete, as long as the full report arrives within the specified period, with the quality unit signing the release record afterward
options.D: After receipt it must first be quarantined until it has been tested or examined and released before use

questions.explanation: Section 211.82 requires that each lot of components, containers, and closures be quarantined after receipt and before testing, until it has been tested or examined and released. Completion of sampling or a normal appearance does not equal release.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.84, what must be done at a minimum when testing each component of a drug product?

options.A: At least one purity test, with identity replaceable by the supplier's label information
options.B: At least one test to verify identity, and if a specific identity test is available, it must be used
options.C: At least one microbiological test to confirm that the component is free of any objectionable microorganisms
options.D: A single assay is enough, with responsibility for identity borne by the supplier and no separate test performed by the manufacturer

questions.explanation: Section 211.84 provides that at least one test to verify the identity of each component must be conducted, and that a specific identity test must be used if one exists. Purity, assay, or microbiological tests cannot replace identity testing.

questions.question: A manufacturer wants to replace its own full testing of a component with the supplier's report of analysis. Under 21 CFR 211.84, what conditions must be met?

options.A: The supplier is a long-standing vendor with no history of quality problems, in which case the report can be accepted directly, with only a yearly written confirmation by purchasing and no testing
options.B: The manufacturer must repeat all items in the report for every lot, with the supplier report serving only as a comparison reference
options.C: The manufacturer performs at least one specific identity test and establishes the reliability of the supplier's analyses through appropriate validation at appropriate intervals
options.D: Only the supplier's GMP certificate and report need to be obtained, and the manufacturer need not conduct any testing or validation

questions.explanation: Section 211.84 allows acceptance of a supplier's report, but the manufacturer must conduct at least one specific identity test and periodically establish the reliability of the supplier's analyses through appropriate validation. Neither no testing at all nor full retesting of every lot is what the provision requires.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.87, in what circumstances must approved components, containers, and closures be retested or reexamined and approved or rejected by the QCU?

options.A: As necessary, for example after prolonged storage, or after exposure to air, heat, or other conditions that might adversely affect them
options.B: Only when the supplier changes its company address or manufacturing site name
options.C: Before every issue to production, regardless of storage period or exposure conditions, and approved by the production department
options.D: Only after the finished product has failed, when the materials used in it must be retested

questions.explanation: Section 211.87 requires retesting as necessary, for example after prolonged storage or exposure to air, heat, or other conditions that may affect quality, with approval or rejection by the QCU in accordance with the procedures for new materials.

questions.question: What does 21 CFR 211.89 require for rejected components, drug product containers, and closures?

options.A: After being labeled "rejected," they may be stored in the same area as accepted material to save warehouse space and handling time, with the reason and date of rejection written on the label for the warehouse's reference
options.B: They must be identified and controlled under a quarantine system designed to prevent their use in manufacturing or processing operations for which they are unsuitable
options.C: They must all be destroyed on the same day, with no quantity retained and no records of their disposition or lot information
options.D: The production manager decides whether to reuse them in another product, and quarantine is unnecessary as long as the finished product passes final testing

questions.explanation: Section 211.89 requires that rejected materials be identified and controlled under a quarantine system, to prevent their use in operations for which they are unsuitable. Mixing them with accepted material or allowing production to reassign them on its own violates this intent.

questions.question: A warehouse holds labels for two strengths of the same drug and labels for a different dosage form. Under 21 CFR 211.122, how should these labels be stored?

options.A: Labels for different strengths of the same drug may be mixed on the same shelf and distinguished by label color
options.B: Arranged in order of arrival date, and all production and packaging personnel may take them at any time, with each department head deciding who may enter the storage area
options.C: Labels for different products, strengths, dosage forms, or quantity of contents must be stored separately with suitable identification, and access limited to authorized personnel
options.D: Only labels for different drugs must be separated, and different strengths or dosage forms of the same drug may be stored together in the same area

questions.explanation: Section 211.122 requires that labels and labeling materials for each different drug product, strength, dosage form, or quantity of contents be stored separately with suitable identification, and that access to the storage area be limited to authorized personnel. Storing different strengths or dosage forms together, or arranging by arrival date with open access, creates a mix-up risk.

questions.question: Labels for two strengths of the same drug are printed together on the same sheet (gang-printed labeling). Under 21 CFR 211.122, under what condition may this be used?

options.A: The labels cut from the sheet can be adequately differentiated by size, shape, or color for the different drugs or strengths
options.B: As long as every label on the sheet is printed with the lot number, with no other visual differentiation needed
options.C: As long as two people on the packaging line cross-check each other, with no visual differentiation required
options.D: It may be used in any case, with only a note in the batch production record that gang-printed labeling was used

questions.explanation: Section 211.122 in principle prohibits gang-printed labeling for different drug products or different strengths or quantities of contents of the same drug, unless the labeling cut from the sheet is adequately differentiated by size, shape, or color. A lot number or after-the-fact cross-checking cannot replace visual differences.

questions.question: When cut labeling is used, under 21 CFR 211.122, what must be stated on the container holding the cut labels to prevent mix-ups?

options.A: Only the drug name, with the remaining information recorded in the batch production record and no need to put it on the container
options.B: The name of the label printer and the print date, so that the label source and lot can later be traced to the supplier, without stating the drug strength or quantity of contents to which the labels belong
options.C: The drug name and expiration date, with the lot number added later in the batch production record rather than on the container
options.D: The name, strength, quantity of contents, and lot or control number of the drug product to which the labels belong

questions.explanation: Section 211.122 requires the container of cut labeling to identify the drug product, its strength, quantity of contents, and the lot or control number of the drug product to which it belongs, and requires that labels for different drugs and strengths be stored in separate areas or physically segregated, all to prevent mix-ups.

questions.question: 21 CFR 211.125 requires procedures to control label issuance. What is the purpose?

options.A: Only to track label printing costs and to simplify month-end settlement of label accounts and quantities with the supplier
options.B: To prevent labeling errors and to allow reconciliation of the quantities issued, used, and returned
options.C: To let production staff take extra labels for backup on their own, avoiding packaging line stoppages due to label shortages, with the production leader requesting replenishment from the warehouse at the end of each shift
options.D: To ensure that all issued labels are used up on the same day, with any unused labels destroyed the same day

questions.explanation: The purpose of 211.125 is to control the issuance of labeling in order to prevent errors, and to provide a basis for reconciliation. Taking extra labels as backup increases the risk of using the wrong labels, which is contrary to the purpose of controlled issuance.

questions.question: After a batch has been packaged, the quantities of labels issued, used, and returned cannot be reconciled with the number of units processed. Under 21 CFR 211.125, how should this be handled?

options.A: The discrepancy must be investigated, and the quantities of labeling issued, used, and returned must be reconciled with the number of units processed
options.B: As long as the finished product looks correct, the batch can be released directly after the difference is noted in the batch record
options.C: The difference in labels is regarded as wastage and discarded by packaging staff themselves, with no investigation record needed
options.D: The difference is made up by drawing extra labels at the next batch of packaging, with no separate action required for this batch

questions.explanation: Section 211.125 requires reconciliation of the quantities of labeling issued, used, and returned against the number of units processed, and any discrepancy found must be investigated. Missing labels may mean the wrong product is mixed in, and the gap cannot be handled by estimation or by making it up afterward.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.125, under what condition may reconciliation of cut or gang-printed labeling be waived?

options.A: The labeling is already printed with the lot number and expiration date, and its layout has been approved in advance by the quality unit
options.B: The batch's packaging quantity is less than half that of other batches, and the packaging line operators are experienced
options.C: The labeling is examined 100% during the labeling operation to confirm that the labels used are all correct
options.D: A portion of the labeled units has been checked by QC on a sampling basis, and the check found no errors

questions.explanation: The waiver condition in 211.125 is that cut or gang-printed labeling is examined 100% at the same time as the labeling operation. Having the lot number printed, a smaller batch size, or a sampling check is not enough for a waiver.

questions.question: Packaging and labeling of two different drug products must be done in the same plant. Under 21 CFR 211.130, how should this be arranged to prevent mix-ups and cross-contamination?

options.A: As long as the outer packaging colors of the two products differ, they can run simultaneously on the same line without separation
options.B: Separate the operations from those for other drugs by physical or spatial means
options.C: As long as the packaging materials are printed with their own product names, no physical or spatial separation is needed
options.D: Operators visually confirm that every packaging unit is correct during the operation, which can replace separation arrangements even if the operations of the two products are set up in the same space

questions.explanation: Section 211.130 requires physical or spatial separation from operations on other drugs to prevent mix-ups and cross-contamination. Packaging color, product names, or visual confirmation cannot replace segregation.

questions.topic: Examination of packaging materials before use
questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.130, what must be done with packaging and labeling materials before packaging operations begin, and how is it recorded?

options.A: Only verify that the quantity issued is correct and report the result to the supervisor verbally, with no written record
options.B: Check their suitability only after packaging is complete, and record the result in the equipment log rather than the batch production record
options.C: Replace the check with the supplier's shipping inspection report, with no inspection of materials in the plant before packaging
options.D: Inspect them for suitability and correctness before packaging operations, and document the inspection in the batch production record

questions.explanation: Section 211.130 requires that packaging and labeling materials be inspected for suitability and correctness before packaging operations, and that the inspection be documented in the batch production record; after-the-fact sampling or reliance on supplier reports alone cannot catch the problem before the wrong materials are used.

questions.question: After the previous batch is packaged, a small amount of finished product from the old batch and unsuitable labeling materials remain on the packaging line, and the next batch is about to begin. Under 21 CFR 211.130, what must be done before the next batch begins?

options.A: As long as the labels of the new batch have been issued correctly, the residue from the old batch can be dealt with in passing during packaging
options.B: The operator clears the residue on their own, with no check by another person and no written record
options.C: Inspect the packaging and labeling facilities immediately before use to ensure that drug products and unsuitable materials from previous operations have been removed, and document this in the batch production record
options.D: Check and record after this batch is packaged, dealing with any residue separately only if it is found during the process, and if residue is found merely note it in the batch record without removing it

questions.explanation: This provision of 211.130 is line clearance: the packaging and labeling facilities are inspected immediately before use to ensure that drug products and unsuitable packaging and labeling materials from previous operations have been removed, and the result must be documented in the batch production record. A check afterward cannot prevent residue from causing mix-ups.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.132, how is a tamper-evident package defined?

options.A: One having one or more indicators or barriers to entry which, if breached or missing, can reasonably be expected to provide visible evidence to consumers that tampering has occurred
options.B: A package completely covered with opaque material so that consumers and distribution personnel cannot directly see the contents, regardless of whether visible traces are left after the package is breached
options.C: A package printed with an anti-counterfeit barcode that must be read by dedicated scanning equipment to determine whether the package has been opened
options.D: A package that can be opened only with special tools, so that ordinary consumers cannot open it themselves before purchase

questions.explanation: The key point of the definition in 211.132 is that, if breached or missing, it can provide visible evidence of tampering to consumers. Whether the package is opaque, has a barcode, or needs special tools to open is not the defining criterion.

questions.question: After packaging and labeling are complete, under 21 CFR 211.134, how should representative units be sampled and examined to confirm correct labeling, and how are the results handled?

options.A: Sample a few units for visual inspection before packaging begins, with a verbal report to the supervisor being enough, and no need to check other units as long as the sampled units are correctly labeled
options.B: Check only the label on the last outer carton, with no need to record the result of this check if it looks correct
options.C: Cross-check the whole batch only against computer records, with no visual examination of any actual finished product units
options.D: At completion of finishing operations, take a representative sample of units and visually examine them for correct labeling, recording the results in the batch production or control records

questions.explanation: Section 211.134 requires that a representative sample of units be taken at the completion of finishing operations and visually examined for correct labeling, with the results recorded in the batch production or control records. A pre-packaging spot check, looking only at the outer carton, or checking only computer data cannot confirm the labeling of finished units.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.137, how should the expiration date on a drug product's labeling be determined?

options.A: Set by the marketing department according to market demand and sales cycle, then approved by the QCU at release
options.B: Determined from the results of appropriate stability testing described in 211.166, to assure that the drug product meets applicable standards at the time of use
options.C: Always a fixed three years from the manufacturing date, with no need to adjust between products based on their own test results
options.D: Provided by the packaging material supplier based on the durability of the container, with the manufacturer adopting the supplier's date directly whether or not the manufacturer has any stability data

questions.explanation: Section 211.137 requires drug products to bear an expiration date determined by appropriate stability testing (211.166), to assure that they meet the applicable standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity at the time of use. Marketing needs or a fixed number of years are not the basis.

questions.question: If actual laboratory practice deviates from the written specifications, standards, sampling plans, or test procedures, how should this be handled under 21 CFR 211.160?

options.A: It must be recorded and justified, and documented at the time of performance
options.B: It need only be summarized in the annual quality review, with no need to record it on the spot each time a deviation occurs, and a deviation needs no justification as long as the direct supervisor approves it verbally afterward
options.C: As long as the final test result passes, the deviation need not be recorded and no justification is needed
options.D: The analyst decides on their own and notifies colleagues verbally, with no QCU review or written record

questions.explanation: Section 211.160 requires laboratory controls to be documented at the time of performance, and any deviation must be recorded and justified. A passing result does not mean the deviation may go unrecorded.

questions.question: After calibration according to the calibration program, an instrument is found not to meet the established accuracy limits. How should the instrument be handled under 21 CFR 211.160?

options.A: It may continue to be used, as long as each test report notes that the instrument's calibration result was outside the limits
options.B: It may be downgraded to non-critical tests but must not be used for tests related to finished product release
options.C: After adjustment it can be used immediately for release testing, without reconfirming accuracy and without keeping records
options.D: An instrument that does not meet the established specifications must not be used, and the calibration program must provide remedial action when limits are not met

questions.explanation: Section 211.160 requires a written calibration program that includes accuracy and precision limits and remedial action when the limits are not met, and prohibits use of instruments, apparatus, gauges, and recording devices that do not meet established specifications.

questions.question: Under 21 CFR 211.165, what must laboratory determination confirm for each batch of drug product before release?

options.A: Only appearance and package integrity, with the other quality attributes confirmed by the production department itself during packaging
options.B: Satisfactory conformance to final specifications, including the identity and strength of each active ingredient
options.C: Only that the stability study has been initiated, with no laboratory determination of the batch's final specifications needed at release
options.D: Only the sterility test result is needed, with the other specification items replaced by the supplier's shipping inspection report, and conformance to final specifications judged by the production unit at the packaging stage

questions.explanation: Section 211.165 requires that, before release, each batch be confirmed by laboratory determination to conform to final specifications, including the identity and strength of each active ingredient. Appearance, the start of stability testing, or a single sterility result is not enough.

questions.topic: Acceptance criteria and statistical quality control
questions.question: What does 21 CFR 211.165 require of the acceptance criteria used by the QCU for sampling and testing?

options.A: A single pass or fail result is sufficient, with no statistical quality control criteria to accompany it
options.B: They are set by the production department based on experience, and the QCU need only check that the records are complete at release
options.C: They must be adequate to assure that batches conform to each specification and to appropriate statistical quality control criteria, with the criteria including appropriate acceptance and rejection levels
options.D: Only a rejection level needs to be set, and the QCU decides the acceptance level itself after testing, based on the results of the batch

questions.explanation: Section 211.165 requires that acceptance criteria be adequate to ensure that batches conform to each applicable specification and appropriate statistical quality control criteria, and that the statistical criteria include appropriate acceptance and/or rejection levels, not decided after the fact.

questions.question: A batch of drug product fails to meet established standards or specifications on testing. Under 21 CFR 211.165, which of the following is correct?

options.A: The batch can be released directly with the approval of the QCU head, with the reason noted in the batch record, and without any additional investigation or follow-up action on the batch
options.B: It can be downgraded and sold for another use at a customer's request, without retesting or any further treatment
options.C: It must in no case be reprocessed and can only be destroyed entirely, because the regulation does not allow any form of reprocessing
options.D: It must be rejected; reprocessing may be performed, but the reprocessed material must meet standards and specifications before it is accepted

questions.explanation: Section 211.165 provides that a drug product failing to meet standards must be rejected, and reprocessing may be performed, but the reprocessed material must meet appropriate standards, specifications, and other relevant criteria before being accepted and used.
